This Refurb Weekend is a sequel in two ways.
[Six years ago](/2020/06/refurb-weekend-alpha-micro-eagle-300.html) I fixed the power supply and case fan in my 68EC030-based Alpha Microsystems Eagle 300, a more modernized and substantially faster Alpha Micro running AMOS, their unique DEC-inspired multiuser operating system. These blue-collar boxes were very common in many vertical markets due to their tightly integrated business-specific software packages, and are especially unusual for running their big-endian 68000-series processors _little_-endian (for data file backwards compatibility with their WD-16 ancestors). The 1990s-era Alpha Micro Eagle family improves on the originals with later 68K and even ColdFire CPUs, plus Ethernet and faster SCSI.
The second way it's a sequel is to [our previous Alpha Micro refurb weekend](/2026/03/refurb-weekend-double-header-alpha.html), a double header restoring an Alpha Micro AM-1000 and AM-1200, two members of Alpha Micro's most popular series of computers and some of the closest things they made in the early '80s to desktop workstations.
From the outside, the Eagle comes in a PC-style case, but it's not a PC:
[![](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhtxXh6ipOCrGK54Zsl5U0tbOrL7jLHeBbGPf766eyl_M2XO_OdG7O_oqStkg8TBzXiW-towqKCGHfvAFiQT-9wVV2jkYw8TIEXZ24qJ4vR8lcy23R-v3Ma6idK4ObQRthAfID7v9JeUsfxa1k-OJNI8JkRhs4UQqzJOGOE47N7rDTEQP9nDuP5VoVyX5Y/s320/PXL_20261004_143856069.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhtxXh6ipOCrGK54Zsl5U0tbOrL7jLHeBbGPf766eyl_M2XO_OdG7O_oqStkg8TBzXiW-towqKCGHfvAFiQT-9wVV2jkYw8TIEXZ24qJ4vR8lcy23R-v3Ma6idK4ObQRthAfID7v9JeUsfxa1k-OJNI8JkRhs4UQqzJOGOE47N7rDTEQP9nDuP5VoVyX5Y/s3648/PXL_20261004_143856069.jpg)
This particular Eagle 300, with a 40MHz 68EC030 CPU, runs `ampm.floodgap.com` using the webserver provided with AlphaTCP — yes, Alpha Micros [can be networked](/2020/09/hacking-gopher-client-into-alpha-micro.html) — and its own on-board Ethernet. At the time the cooling fan failure was putting a lot of strain on the hard disk because it was overheating, and since this was my first Alpha Micro and I wanted to keep it in good nick, I decided I would put a SCSI2SD in it after the repair and get rid of the spinning disk entirely. Fast-forward to last fall, a little over a year ago, when I tried to do exactly that with a ZuluSCSI.
And then it wouldn't start.
[![](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhmTPjhLcwjhOwGfqm_KF9N0kxGAO0J2V_XuFcnPvHAd2Ubz5HXsxoRIG-n0qexU4WYkhVK7d1fRfzZdGHSK4DMlpsy0zV0MHNx3vwyxikRn4NUbkhwntxNH2V6qOJ6TcmlCgDfqN0is0AYn4tBuUk7MHz6dL8-grGoJS7yG6VBzouXRcPjFf0_1dhg7-Q/s320/PXL_20250904_023117154.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhmTPjhLcwjhOwGfqm_KF9N0kxGAO0J2V_XuFcnPvHAd2Ubz5HXsxoRIG-n0qexU4WYkhVK7d1fRfzZdGHSK4DMlpsy0zV0MHNx3vwyxikRn4NUbkhwntxNH2V6qOJ6TcmlCgDfqN0is0AYn4tBuUk7MHz6dL8-grGoJS7yG6VBzouXRcPjFf0_1dhg7-Q/s4080/PXL_20250904_023117154.jpg)
It would power on, but it wouldn't enter the boot sequence, not even with the old hard disk back in it, not even to run the internal self-test. I was worried I'd negligently blown one of its two main system boards and that meant I needed another. This entry took as long as it did to come to fruition because Eagles in general aren't easy to find, and on top of that I was looking for a specific one. Through a couple of referrals I managed to get what I _thought_ was a replacement unit I could raid for parts, but it turned out to be something rather more special — and then I was even more fortunate when I got the Eagle 300 back out of storage to make one last attempt at reviving it.
To cap it off we'll go stick ZuluSCSIs in everybody else, including my Motorola ColdFire-based Eagle 450, the first ColdFire server ever produced and what _used_ to be the fastest Eagle in the house until the new hotness came. I even converted the external BlueSCSI the AM-1200 was using to an internal ZuluSCSI too. Now nearly everybody's got a solid-state boot disk and they're all a good bit more zippy, so we'll gawk at the internals, compare 68K CPU and storage benchmarks and most importantly learn from my mistakes, because as my late father always said, "I'd rather be lucky than good." On a more solemn note, we'll also observe a moment of silence for one of the line's creators who passed away last year. It's time for a Refurb Multi-Weekend Sequel.
[![](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgoGLAb62uyPYNpZ-3N-Up4QJ7ivBGf7Mk-uGnaMHQ7horUMnlYNJTht9TRNHVxpAEK8pefQZeJkleBS2MNsAJmpgGJkPGYnVJBCylhgdFHsghB5AfbfmvGE5u0AAvKFBD3Q90yGM-hO2EiRXj-esHt1Mc_qAVCF2jhtCFfmUiXkwl0s9ttOi8r6Nzf-Zo/s320/am1kad.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgoGLAb62uyPYNpZ-3N-Up4QJ7ivBGf7Mk-uGnaMHQ7horUMnlYNJTht9TRNHVxpAEK8pefQZeJkleBS2MNsAJmpgGJkPGYnVJBCylhgdFHsghB5AfbfmvGE5u0AAvKFBD3Q90yGM-hO2EiRXj-esHt1Mc_qAVCF2jhtCFfmUiXkwl0s9ttOi8r6Nzf-Zo/s3014/am1kad.jpg)
Alpha Microsystems, founded in Orange County, California in 1977, produced what were considered some of the earliest "poor man's minicomputers," smaller and more affordable multi-user systems that run a bespoke, Digital Equipment Corporation-influenced operating system named AMOS. In our previous entry we discussed [their history in detail](/2026/03/refurb-weekend-double-header-alpha.html). First-generation Alpha Micros like the AM-100, designed by Dick Wilcox who also wrote most of the operating system, used large S-100 cases and a CPU chipset called the WD-16, derived from the Western Digital MCP-1600 chipset — the same one used in DEC's LSI-11 CPU — but with higher performance microcode developed by Rich Notari. These machines thoroughly outclassed low-end PDP-11s yet were substantially cheaper, and Alpha Micro found a ready audience initially with hobbyists and then later corporate turnkey environments, where its integrated AlphaBASIC and database functionality gave it a competitive advantage. As the WD-16 had little elbow room to evolve, in 1982 Alpha Micro introduced new systems based on the Motorola 68000, porting AlphaBASIC and AMOS to run natively, but swapping address lines to make it appear little-endian for compatibility with WD-16 data files and AlphaBASIC P-code. These new machines included [the AM-1000](/2026/03/refurb-weekend-double-header-alpha.html), Alpha Micro's most popular single model, and by 1984 it constituted the majority of the over 20,000 Alpha Micro machines then in active use.
[![](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiMZC9dxjdp0l_edqXabKOjO89Fl4YfWQ0D1bhXfZ42-uQrFo51_a-LyCP8WB9hczWR4k_t_MPfa9_8Zp-DBZUHiYdRZf84mdbiDCgyyYcJA-ss3uvtnwlG3uxoeAjxcKxSPiDqtfKM2J5DG0Z3WCd45cdL8YHKvaLl2S5a1SKcG2ssU2Src-UTtmB8oqI/s320/am1042ead.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiMZC9dxjdp0l_edqXabKOjO89Fl4YfWQ0D1bhXfZ42-uQrFo51_a-LyCP8WB9hczWR4k_t_MPfa9_8Zp-DBZUHiYdRZf84mdbiDCgyyYcJA-ss3uvtnwlG3uxoeAjxcKxSPiDqtfKM2J5DG0Z3WCd45cdL8YHKvaLl2S5a1SKcG2ssU2Src-UTtmB8oqI/s2309/am1042ead.jpg)
An idealized Alpha Micro office from the 1980s might look like this photo, from their actual advertising of the period. The main system is an AM-1042E, the S-100 box sitting on the pedestal next to the printer, using an AM-100/L CPU with an 8MHz 68000 (the same as the AM-1000, which was integrated into a desktop case), and in the factory-standard configuration shipped with 512K of RAM and a 60MB Winchester ST-506 hard disk. The system served some number of local users connected directly via serial ports, in this case the two administrative assistants with AM-60 terminals (a modified and rebadged Wyse WY-100). The fact everyone here was in the same room with the machine was helpful, because AMOS is a strictly real-memory operating system and executable code ran from where it was loaded in the user's fixed memory allocation — there was no memory protection. Although the admin assistants' explicit permissions were limited by which account they were logged into, using the same style of project-programmer numbers as DEC (e.g., \[1,2\] being the operator account), an errant job of theirs could readily stomp on another and it was not rare for busy systems with buggy software to regularly crash. On the other hand, this also made it fast and efficient with little separation between you and the hardware, and even Alpha Micros with fairly modest specifications could support hundreds of simultaneous users.
Alpha Microsystems tried multiple times to broaden the line technologically, though these efforts were largely for naught. Early attempts to put equivalent hardware onto a PC ISA co-processor card, with software to interchange between MS-DOS and AMOS, yielded only an expensive and poorly-selling PC that wasn't good at either OS (eventually the company gave up producing turnkey systems and just sold the card). In 1984 Alpha Micro introduced UNIMOS, a licensed version of AT&T System V UNIX which ran on modified AM-1000 hardware with an MMU, but it was likewise too expensive and garnered little interest from new users nor demand from existing ones. The cost of its development, the Unix license and its associated royalties, and a simultaneous lawsuit from DEC over AMOS's similarities subsequently caused lasting damage to the company, and by the end of the decade Alpha Micro found itself almost entirely dependent on legacy AMOS users. In the wake of Wilcox's 1990 retirement and original investor Bob Hitchcock's own departure in 1991, new management tried once more with Unix systems based on the Motorola 88000 — which Motorola abandoned shortly afterwards for the PowerPC AIM alliance, and so no hardware ever shipped.
[![](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEh0eVefdpjZwq_AvWEIDT5501TzLcc54gERDMOWAHe3BTVYCXY7UkbhDIkgq6iePFgrYVVEO5YL6Ne-c47Qb5j4e5o2BbGzumgvO5IGzNdUu7-B2mKvJwIWPAHqx8ZXCpkbcMGCEQaC0NBQjWejEDyAVXs4ADYLJpqsYcH_7uyBjT7f7XCIab9oiY6tlX4/s320/rrart.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEh0eVefdpjZwq_AvWEIDT5501TzLcc54gERDMOWAHe3BTVYCXY7UkbhDIkgq6iePFgrYVVEO5YL6Ne-c47Qb5j4e5o2BbGzumgvO5IGzNdUu7-B2mKvJwIWPAHqx8ZXCpkbcMGCEQaC0NBQjWejEDyAVXs4ADYLJpqsYcH_7uyBjT7f7XCIab9oiY6tlX4/s2048/rrart.jpg)
If the platform couldn't be migrated, reasoned Alpha Micro leadership, then it would have to be modernized. A solution was needed for two problems in particular: more up-to-date yet less expensive and fully backwards-compatible hardware for new sales from their risk-averse userbase, and an upgrade path to entice users flatly refusing to part with their old machines. Up to this point, system upgradability had been somewhat uneven and highly model-dependent. RAM and serial port upgrades were generally bespoke boards made from discrete parts which were tedious to replace and repair. Although Alpha Micro had been quick to incorporate Motorola's subsequent 68K CPUs, these higher-performance processors generally only appeared in their larger, more expensive server systems (with the notable exception of the '020, first in the AM-2000 but later in the AM-1600, notionally a desktop computer). Some machines could be upgraded with board swaps, though this wasn't particularly cost-effective, and at the time the most popular AM-1000 and slightly upgraded AM-1200 systems had no official upgrade path from Alpha Micro at all. The December 1987 AM-3000 was the first 68030 machine available from _anybody_ — yes, really, just two months after the '030's October introduction — initially offering a 20MHz CPU, 32K of L2 cache and supporting up to 360 simultaneous terminals, but even the lowliest 30-user configuration started north of $40,000 \[about $117,600 in 2026 dollars\]. By contrast, Alpha Micro was uncharacteristically tardy in adopting the 68040 and didn't release the 33MHz AM-4000 until 1993. It was nevertheless nearly as expensive, and for most small offices, which were now increasingly Alpha Micro's financial anchor, that kind of money was simply beyond consideration.
In 1993 the company settled on a two-board approach to solve both problems at once. The CPU board, dubbed the Roadrunner and designed by engineer Joshua Stumpf, contained the new processor, standard RAM SIMM slots, L2 cache (if present), and SCSI controller. This board was specifically designed to also fit in legacy machines, specifically the desktop AM-1000, AM-1200 and AM-1600 and server AM-2000 and AM-3000 systems, and initially came in a 68030 and two 68040 versions. A second board served as the CPU board's system interface, linked together using a custom "X-BUS" interconnect over twin 34-pin cables. For legacy installs, this second board was an active interposer physically replacing the original processor, which in elderly units sometimes needed to be desoldered (though that was also true for the few third-party CPU upgrades then extant, like InterLink's Dimension-030, so the Roadrunner was at least no worse). But this second board could be a whole new system architecture of its own, and that was what the I/O board was, designed by Rod Hewitt. It carried the power supply connectors, controlled the system front panel, contained the System Security Device for licensing (more on this later), presented built-in external ports for parallel, SCSI and (for certain loadouts) Ethernet, had an internal port for an optional floppy drive, and provided SIMM-format "paddle card" slots for option cards. Best of all, these boards were smaller and — by using off-the-shelf commodity hardware — cheaper to manufacture, and could be paired into multiple configurations, together becoming the company's long-promised updated low-end and mid-range systems.
[![](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjOYSoNPVEPAGRYoXPalenr1L_tqepE_uapnHsNxBF1qciGXzukEl3hfCfGMumFYNigjU8D0oT4naOwYksHGbqoIwge-vMqUjCE2Z4aalYIkZz9eSD28Qv_hkW0nDbAxpKc2lmrKXEwm35qRctFmfuj5-sodH5gSIyFReD7RSTCgnG_4u8zwFi_94he2LM/s320/eaglead.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjOYSoNPVEPAGRYoXPalenr1L_tqepE_uapnHsNxBF1qciGXzukEl3hfCfGMumFYNigjU8D0oT4naOwYksHGbqoIwge-vMqUjCE2Z4aalYIkZz9eSD28Qv_hkW0nDbAxpKc2lmrKXEwm35qRctFmfuj5-sodH5gSIyFReD7RSTCgnG_4u8zwFi_94he2LM/s2048/eaglead.jpg)
In 1994, the new architecture launched — or perhaps I should say took flight, as the Alpha Micro Eagle family. These earliest systems shared a common PC-type minitower deskside case which was also used for a reworked AM-1600LC desktop system and the AM-950 486DX2/66 PC. The central model was the Eagle 300, powered by a 40MHz 68EC030 CPU board (remember, AMOS doesn't need an MMU) and an I/O board with SCSI-2, two parallel ports and Ethernet, plus four paddlecard slots for up to 32 serial ports. The Eagle 400 was correspondingly the same I/O system board with a 33MHz (billed as 66MHz because of the '040's double-speed secondary clock, to be discussed in the second half) full 68040 CPU board and 32K of L2 cache; the Eagle 500 had a 40MHz (80MHz) one. But their best attribute was the price: unlike the big AM systems, these machines started at just a few thousand dollars, depending on license caps, and they'd run all your old software.
If that was still too expensive for you, the company added two more choices that were even cheaper. One was the Eagle 200, which mated the 68EC030 CPU board with a cut-down system board missing Ethernet, one of the parallel ports and two of the paddlecard slots. In November the lowest-end Eagle 100 dispensed with the modularity of the other systems entirely, consolidating the 68EC030 CPU and I/O boards into a single logic board also designed by Hewitt with eight built-in serial ports, no standard Ethernet (offered through a paddlecard upgrade, which I'll show you), only one parallel port and only one paddlecard slot. As promised, Alpha Micro also offered legacy upgrade packages using the same Roadrunner CPU boards, sold separately with their system-specific active interposers for existing installations.
[![](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgB9Z8ou6CC7m93vCLUs2nS-O8qOo8MKR8uScKzV7GHnwGJALWHjhQApNu2nS9_sVYyWa45bPfy-_ypYuPTS_IYooWBAM-da_byuO7Qa3PKYwnmSYC552SemyHGAqMtblLJfkRF4tAr1Uri_Z5XuFx_t0K7QP_Jrkzk-GRrosaSLpJ749sGRIxvaB701Es/s320/DSCN7891.JPG)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgB9Z8ou6CC7m93vCLUs2nS-O8qOo8MKR8uScKzV7GHnwGJALWHjhQApNu2nS9_sVYyWa45bPfy-_ypYuPTS_IYooWBAM-da_byuO7Qa3PKYwnmSYC552SemyHGAqMtblLJfkRF4tAr1Uri_Z5XuFx_t0K7QP_Jrkzk-GRrosaSLpJ749sGRIxvaB701Es/s2048/DSCN7891.JPG)
This is my own Eagle 300, shown here when I unpacked it in my apartment in 2007. It came in the standard four 5.25" bay case shared by all five initial configurations, which I was delighted to note was little-yellowed and even now nearly two decades later is still largely unblemished. The case was not custom-built for Alpha Micro and was merely an off-the-shelf one they bought in bulk, though I have not yet found the OEM. This computer was my first fully operational Alpha Micro; I had always intended to own one personally for [reasons I've related elsewhere](/2026/03/refurb-weekend-double-header-alpha.html), and I managed to land it for just a couple hundred bucks in fully working order. (Boy, are those days gone.)
Based on the software still on the hard disk, this machine was previously used at a chain of three party stores in Washington state as a centralised rental and point-of-sale system, a common turnkey application. On arrival it sported the same loadout as in this article's first picture except for its original smaller-capacity Tandberg QIC tape drive, which in Alpha Micro parlance is called a tape streamer. Since these systems don't boot from CD, QIC tape is your only way to cold start and restore most 68K Alpha Micro computers if the hard disk fails. These systems also don't support the old Alpha Micro VHS backup system, hopefully to be the subject [of a future article](/search/label/vcr), which was ubiquitous in their early hardware. There is a single hard disk in the second 5.25" bay, though these first-generation systems also supported 5.25" and 3.5" floppy drives using an AM-219 controller board.
[![](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjy_fz0w3VFirVSGA6WxjdxQT7Xqry48NttIhXWHifwRML6LECUBrcC7ZN-2Om_yV1wMwu7PEmOJJsDCcHhxKI5ui17Fe_3skPTcRhnQ1ln77EbMiPV01asWLTKzK7xPrHz0iI0YiefmNxLTl5iclil-KztXixc0AorfvG11Ns6XQQQcwu1Y0Zev39H7c0/s320/PXL_20250904_023011942.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjy_fz0w3VFirVSGA6WxjdxQT7Xqry48NttIhXWHifwRML6LECUBrcC7ZN-2Om_yV1wMwu7PEmOJJsDCcHhxKI5ui17Fe_3skPTcRhnQ1ln77EbMiPV01asWLTKzK7xPrHz0iI0YiefmNxLTl5iclil-KztXixc0AorfvG11Ns6XQQQcwu1Y0Zev39H7c0/s4080/PXL_20250904_023011942.jpg)
Pictures of the case in other Alpha Micro marketing literature showed two "badge" areas which contained the vendor logo and, improbably, a little LCD clock. (This appears to have been stock photography from the OEM; perhaps that tidbit jogs someone's memory about the case.) For the Eagles, Alpha Micro commissioned two customized metal badges for those areas which are seen on most members of the line. They look very nice and give it a pro feeling.

The backplate shows the system's vital statistics. Although collectively the family are called Eagles, the internal designation for the Eagle 300 is the AM-3500-E300 (so the E400 would be the AM-3500-E400, and so forth, reflecting their common ancestry), implying it slotted between their AM-3000 and AM-4000 large systems. It is serial #02233 with a stated manufacturing date of January 1998, relatively late in the model's lifespan. This particular machine might have been a warranty replacement because the system initialization file indicates they took delivery of the system in December 1997 and the serial in that file is slightly earlier (#02200).
The plate sticker also carries the SSD serial number as shipped from the factory, or System Security Device (not to be confused with the modern solid-state drive). In [our previous Alpha Micro foray](/2026/03/refurb-weekend-double-header-alpha.html) we discussed the SSD's role, a chip installed in every 68K (and later x86) Alpha Micro, even the earliest S-100 boards, used by the operating system and any installed VAR software packages to enforce copy protection and license caps. The SSD number on the rear is just a serial number, printed on the rear plate for convenience and engraved on the SSD chip inside, which I'll show you in a moment. This number is not the key stored inside the chip, up to 256 bytes in length, which only Alpha Micro recorded. When a VAR wanted to lock an install to a particular system, they would provide their private code to Alpha Micro plus the user's SSD serial number, and Alpha Micro would look up the key and generate an alphanumeric PIC (Product Installation Code) that the VAR either used for direct installation or to provide to the user. During the installation process the PIC (usually irreversibly) encoded a binary overlay for the protected executable(s), making it impossible to run them on a system where the SSD didn't match. To facilitate logic board swaps and upgrades, the SSD is socketed and easily transplanted into a new board, but PICs were expensive then and unobtanium now, another reason hard disk backups were so critical.

Here we have its AM-172 68EC030 CPU board, with a copyright date of 1993, mounted to the bottom of the case in this later unit; early units mounted them vertically on a sidepanel which inconveniently blocked access to the I/O board. In the top left/northwest corner is the SCSI cable, and then the two X-BUS cables. Power is provided by a standard Molex connector stuck in the back betweeen them (remember this detail). On the right/east side is a single SIMM slot containing a 72-pin 16MB parity FPM RAM stick. The AM-172 supports up to 64MB in this slot, though the board needs to be jumpered (at JP5 and JP6) to tell the computer how much is there. The three big chips are the 68EC030 processor, which is socketed and has a date code of 12th week 1997, along with an NCR 53C710 SCSI-2 controller (manufactured by Symbios Logic, 2nd week 1997) supporting 10MB/s synchronous transfers, and a Lattice Semiconductor MACH130 PLD (manufactured by AMD, 8th week 1997), basically four "PAL26V16-equivalent" blocks jammed into one die. The CPU and the 53C710 are both clocked by an 80MHz crystal divided down to 40MHz; there are also 16MHz and 50MHz oscillators on the board which appear to be used for the PLD and bus logic.
Likely for cost reasons there is no L2 cache, though another thing to keep in mind is — so I'm told — that for compatibility reasons with 68000 and 68010-era AMOS software it is not possible to enable the data cache (or at least not without substantial difficulty). In fact, we observed exactly this phenomenon when looking at the driver for [the InterLink Dimension-030 CPU upgrade](/2026/03/refurb-weekend-double-header-alpha.html), which puts a 68030 in an AM-1000: it never set the data cache bit in the '030's CACR at all. Although some machines can accept an external L2 cache, including one we'll look at in detail, anything it would provide is strictly I-cache.

There is no known way to read out the code and/or clone it without cracking it open and there was (allegedly) a cottage industry back in the day that did exactly that. Each card sends off two ribbons to two additional cards installed in the rear (a total of four). These are the 8P8C "RJ-45" ports you saw and are carried on four-port AM-90 "Lightning" boards, consisting of a large array of Zener diodes with one for every active line. As the name implies, they are intended to protect the hardware from high voltage surges on connected terminals, either repelling the excess voltage entirely or limiting damage to the Lightning card itself where the diodes can easily be replaced (there are no other active electronics). In installations with sometimes distant terminals connected by repeater, lightning strikes and other such surges were a non-theoretical risk, so cards like this served as a reasonable insurance policy.
For even larger port concentrations, the AM-318 can directly drive a single RJ-21 Amphenol connector, putting all eight ports on "one" card. Inconveniently the RJ-21 connector requires a breakout cable and is physically identical to a Centronics-style 50-pin SCSI (but is _not_). I have such an example later on.
Other serial paddlecards can also be installed. The AM-314 provides only four serial ports, but is not merely a cut-down AM-318 — the AM-314 can also be configured for RS-422 (the AM-318 is strictly RS-232) and supports all RS-232 handshake lines (the AM-318 only RTS/CTS), and in certain configurations can trigger a remote reboot from a connected distant console by grounding pin 1 with pin 7. By contrast, the more exotic AM-338 provides an IBM Binary Synchronous Communication "Bisync" link, typically used for Remote Job Entry (RJE) or CICS connections with IBM mainframes, but could theoretically have also worked with some early point-to-point networks like BITNET. It connects to an AM-339 which provides the physical port.

When I plugged the CPU board back in and turned the system on again, this code ("2d") showed up. I removed the ZuluSCSI and reconnected the Seagate drive. It still showed up. I removed everything from the SCSI bus. It still showed up. Okay, I said to myself in panic, I must somehow have blown the SCSI controller; maybe I can work around it. I held in the reset button while powering it on to see if I could get it into the ROM self-test. The code still showed up.
I powered it down and consulted the documentation. "If status 2d or 3d remains on the display panel, your computer has encountered an error, perhaps due to faulty memory or addressing. Perform 'Procedure #5: Self-Test \[which is what I just did\].' If your computer does not pass the self test, call your VAR with the information from the test. Stop." Well, that's just dandy. In the list of status codes later on, there is no explicit 2d, just an "xd" where the boot sequence "failed because of a time-out error. This code may indicate faulty memory or an addressing problem." Here the x indicates either the alternate boot device (2), in this case the tape streamer, or the primary boot device (3), in this case the hard disk. The primary and secondary devices are configured by the DIP set on the back, but I hadn't changed those, and even if they needed to be changed for the ZuluSCSI (note from the future: they do), that didn't explain why it wouldn't boot with the original hard disk either.
Given that it couldn't even enter the self-test, there was clearly more wrong than just the SCSI controller. Since it mentioned faulty memory, I did try one of the SGI Indigo²'s 72-pin SIMMs since those are FPM parity also, though I didn't think that was really the problem and as expected it didn't make a difference. It took me a couple hours to calm down because I really like this machine and I'd somehow just killed it doing what should have been a very low-risk upgrade. Sure, I had the E100s and also since acquired a more powerful later model I'll introduce you to momentarily, but this was my _original_.
I dug up Rod's old E-mail to see if there were any clues in it and recalled what he'd said about the PLDs being dynamically reprogrammed on every startup — _from the CPU board_. I also knew from the service manual that the X-BUS cables, the only connection between the I/O board and the CPU board, had to be correctly connected or the service manual warned damage could result. A horrible theory stirred in my head: perhaps I had managed to accidentally corrupt the PLDs by effectively bringing up the I/O board _without_ the CPU board, where the boot PROMs used to reprogram them are located. However, that also suggested a solution — there are many undocumented jumpers on the AM-319 and I wondered if one of them could be used to trigger a clean reset of the programmable logic.

I typed out a message to Rod and it bounced, which brings us to the memorial portion of this post: it turned out Rod Hewitt had passed away just months prior, in March 2025. Although Rod hadn't worked for Alpha Micro in some time, he still maintained a few systems as a hobby, and was the developer of the Windows ZTERM terminal package that specifically supported Alpha Micro terminal emulation (Alpha Micro even used it for their AM-80 Windows CE thin client, which might itself appear [in a future article](/search/label/alpha%20micro)). He also had an interest in digital television, developing TSReader, a way to analyse the MPEG-2 transport streams commonly used for satellite, cable and IPTV transmissions.
ZTERM and in particular TSReader became far and away his most popular software packages. However, a few years prior and unbeknownst to many, he had quietly entrusted a copy of the TSReader source code to a friend officially "just in case," and sold [ZTERM to MicroSabio](https://microsabio.com/zterm/), a long-time Alpha Micro support company that [maintains A-Shell](https://microsabio.com/a-shell/), a way of running AlphaBASIC applications on modern operating systems. The reason became clear later — he was dying, and it was not treatable. The source code for TSReader was duly posted after his passing and [remains today](https://github.com/TSReader) as his most popular legacy. Rest in peace, Rod, and thank you.
Without Rod's guidance, though, there wasn't much more I could think of to do at that point. I unplugged it, pulled the clock battery and let it sit for a couple days to see if that was enough to reset the PLDs, assuming that was the actual problem, and it didn't. It still seemed like it should be repairable if I could only figure out how, but as there was little point in having it sit fruitlessly on the workbench I removed all the remaining cables from the system board and moved the machine to cold storage until I could come up with something else. In the meantime I turned to my alternative system to get `ampm.floodgap.com` back up and running, though to discuss it we need to bring the history forward some more.

The Eagles were well-received by the user base, though by 1996 it became clear that they couldn't serve the very large installations that were becoming curious about them, and there were just too many models to begin with anyway. The E100 was cheap enough that it sold in good numbers, but few customers fell between it and the E300, making the E200, more expensive to sell and manufacture than the E100, obviously superfluous. Likewise, high-end customers interested in the E500 were interested _only_ in the E500: a junior-varsity 68040, which is what the E400 was, didn't have much appeal. Both the E200 and E400 were quietly dropped.
For large installs that required substantial numbers of serial ports, the existing AM-319 board had to be expanded. The revised AM-319-20 board, providing four built-in serial and parallel ports with a UPS monitor port and a higher-performance DP83902 Ethernet NIC, still had two paddlecard slots, but these slots were widened to 60 pins and could now be part of a bus connected to an external chassis. Alpha Micro had long sold the AM-990, a large capacity case (in this image as used for the AM-4000, though I apologise I don't have a better image of it) and the AM-990 Jumbo, which was even larger. A new higher-performance serial card was developed to take advantage of the widened paddlecard slots, an optically-isolated eight-port card called the AM-359. Twelve AM-359s could be installed in the AM-990, yielding 96 ports when connected to a fan-out in one of the AM-319-20's paddlecard slots (the four on-board ones made an even hundred); the Jumbo could take _another_ twelve AM-359s for _another_ 96 ports connected to the second, a whopping total of 196 serial ports when combined with the base four. If you needed even more, the AM-3501 sidecar chassis could take you well beyond. There was no point in supporting the 68EC030 with such a monster: this new Eagle, officially the Eagle 550 Super Eagle, was 68040 or bust.
[![](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhNZDG1q1uSMxrml-8O4jFW-ZdEwLmhUwclMYuKLCONgO_x0qmPkKoE7pasGM5m1rDksJZ45Fj3pwXtxZQHvathKdEE52NMW2lRjhxNmYQwft-hapbKRpBrS3HmcJS9p7QO-r_ZIW6TcS1TrUGdRETAvD3AT1NClWGCoG6hyphenhyphenbzcd-HQGFnhmqNNxTeYRsY/s320/supereagle.png)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhNZDG1q1uSMxrml-8O4jFW-ZdEwLmhUwclMYuKLCONgO_x0qmPkKoE7pasGM5m1rDksJZ45Fj3pwXtxZQHvathKdEE52NMW2lRjhxNmYQwft-hapbKRpBrS3HmcJS9p7QO-r_ZIW6TcS1TrUGdRETAvD3AT1NClWGCoG6hyphenhyphenbzcd-HQGFnhmqNNxTeYRsY/s2588/supereagle.png)
For users that didn't want to go _that_ large, a Super Eagle in the standard case could support up to 60 ports, four on the AM-319-20 and then seven AM-359 cards in the usual position. The E550 Super Eagle additionally came as a separate upgrade kit for the E500 and the few E400s that sold, essentially a system board swap, though when sold as a turnkey system it was always with the 40/80MHz CPU. The E550 introduced a new Seiko timekeeper chip as well which not only maintained the time but also the "CMOS settings," the first Alpha Micro with an on-screen setup utility in ROM allowing boot configuration.
Subsequently the company was tardy once again in adopting Motorola's newest 68K CPU, this time the superscalar 68060, which had come out in 1994 aimed squarely at the Intel Pentium but didn't reach Alpha Micro customers until mid-1997. This took two forms, a new 66MHz '060 Roadrunner upgrade option for the E550 Super Eagle and the AM-4000 (lesser Eagles need not apply), and a new AM-6000 large system. Interestingly, the AM-6000 is strongly based on the E550, reflected in its internal designation as the AM-3500-6000 making it a "stealth" Eagle. The '060 Roadrunner not only included the new CPU but also 64K of L2 cache, support for up to 256MB of RAM in four SIMM slots, and 68-pin Fast and Wide SCSI-2 using the NCR 53C770.

In fall 1997 Alpha Micro proudly announced over a thousand Roadrunner '030 systems alone had been sold, mostly E300s, along with E100s and a smattering of E500s and Super Eagles. However, it was not lost on company management that Motorola believed the 68000 family was fast approaching a performance wall. This was made most clear by their then-enthusiastic participation in the PowerPC AIM alliance, but also the rise of ColdFire, which Motorola had first announced in 1994 as well. ColdFire was in its own way Motorola's oblique admission that 68K was losing desktop competitiveness to x86, an attempt to scale the ISA down to embedded markets where its familiarity could be an asset. Approximately 20% of the instruction set such as BCD and certain addressing modes were eliminated, meaning the canonical ColdFire could not be fully binary-compatible with any extant 68K. On the other hand, such cuts enabled the core to execute nearly every remaining instruction in a single clock cycle, and the initial die was a miniscule 4.4mm² at 0.5μm, a third the size of Motorola's own 68300-series CPU32+.
Some amount of this work was done by altering the microcode of the 68040V, a fully static 68LC040. Mindful that ColdFire's incompatibility might impair adoption, Motorola chose to create a bridge first-generation chip from this altered 68040V where omitted user mode instructions were left in, demonstrated [on die photos](https://www.cpushack.com/2019/11/01/cpu-of-the-day-motorola-mc68040vl/). While the new chip had smaller 2K instruction and 1K data caches than the 68040V, and the MMU was also eliminated, this deviation from spec was still sufficient to run regular 68EC040 code at the user level. Motorola called this first-generation ColdFire chip the MCF5102, produced on a 0.6μm process, and introduced it in 1995 drawing 0.8W at 20MHz and reaching 33MHz. Clock-for-clock there was no way this chip could eclipse an '060, and the emerging "true" ColdFire 520x series couldn't run existing Alpha Micro software, but the MCF5102 was still faster than an '030 and _nearly_ as fast as an '040 — in fact, we'll prove it. On top of that it was cheaper and AMOS didn't need the MMU anyway, making for a plausible mid-range machine that wouldn't imperil (much) sales of the E500 or E550.

In August 1998, Alpha Micro announced their first ColdFire system based on the MCF5102, and near as I can tell was the first ColdFire-based server ever produced. To visually demonstrate its break from the past, the new system got a new, more modern minitower case (also off-the-shelf) with a mix of 5.25" and 3.5" bays but kept the same Eagle badges. Although Rod Hewitt was no longer working full time for Alpha Micro by then, he still had enough of a relationship with the company that they lent him a pre-production model for evaluation, which he received with enthusiasm. Since this is the only E450 I have personally laid my hands on, we will be referring to his comments liberally as a point of comparison, and consequently the E450's history is probably the best documented of any 68K Eagle. It rolled out to users in October at the annual meeting in nearby Riverside, California.
This particular system was a gift from someone who inherited it from an 9-1-1 emergency dispatch centre and wanted to find it a good home, another way that running an Alpha Micro-powered web server has paid off. The ColdFire MCF5102 is in fact hidden behind the drive bays, the only chip with a heatsink, which should tell you it's doing an awful lot of work. How _fast_ is it doing it, though? While Rod's review stated his prerelease system was apparently running at 33MHz, the oscillator closest to the CPU can be seen clearly in this photograph, and it's ... 25MHz. There are no other crystals on the board except for the serial port one you saw earlier, the official marketing announcement has a board layout that also clearly labels this crystal as 25MHz, and nothing in the MCF5102 user's manual says the chip does anything tricky with the clock. As it happens, the _only_ place in Alpha Micro documentation where the E450's CPU speed is given is Rod's review: everywhere else, even the data sheet, simply says it's a ColdFire and nothing more. Since mine is only 14% slower than his, and his had the cache, his can't possibly have been running at 33MHz either. The E450 is a 25MHz ColdFire, full stop.
In a backwards way, however, this is nothing less than validation of how performant early ColdFires could be. Recall that our E300, a 40MHz 68EC030, had a "CX" computing index score on the `SI.LIT` benchmark of 36.9. The same benchmark on this E450 with a 25MHz MCF5102 gets a score of _59.9_, and Rod's with 64K L2 came in at a whopping 68 (Alpha Micro said 68.5; either one is around 14% higher). By contrast, the E550 Super Eagle, with a full 40MHz ("80MHz") 68040 Roadrunner clocked 60% faster _and_ 32K of L2 cache, officially gets ... 79.9 (note from the future: my figure is 83.6) — the full cached-up faster-clocked 68040's performance on the same code is only around 33-40% better, and just 16-22% or so if the E450 has its cache too. Put another way, the CX/MHz ratio of the faster 68040 was right around 2.0, while the CX/MHz ratio of the MCF5102 is _2.4_ without the cache, and almost 2.75 _with_ it.
Likely because the lower clock speed would have looked bad in marketing materials, similar to why General Magic never mentioned the clock speed [of the DataRover 840](/2022/12/magic-cap-from-magic-link-to-datarover.html), Alpha Micro simply chose not to mention it either. Still, this machine's surprising efficiency proves ColdFire, at least early on, definitely had legs. I'm not sure how Rod got it wrong except that an earlier version may indeed have run that part, though with these numbers, if there had ever been a production 33MHz E450 it might have seriously endangered sales of Alpha Micro's remaining '040s — perhaps that's why they didn't use it even though the faster part existed. Best guess is that the AM-138 was originally designed for the 68040 and then quickly retrofitted for ColdFire, leaving the PGA region as an "R&D test point" (as documented).

This is the faster of the two AM-174 CPU boards, the '040 boards for the original two-piece Eagles I mentioned earlier. Although Alpha Micro eagerly billed this AM-174-02 as having an "80MHz" 68040, that sort of marketing is deliberately simplistic. Recall that 68040s take two clock signals, one labeled `Bclk` for the bus clock, and then a second exactly twice as fast labeled `Pclk` as the so-called processor clock. In the 68020 and 68030, which accept a single clock signal, their internal ALU runs at only half the bus speed such that the 40MHz 68EC030 in the Eagle 300 actually has an ALU running at just 20MHz. For the 68040 Motorola removed this limitation to run its ALU at full bus speed, but the chip designers also studied trace data to optimize for the most common instructions, implementing a 7-stage pipeline where most effective address calculations and fetches occur with no penalty. The upshot of this was to cut most instructions' cycle count in half or more.
The 2x processor clock is truly used, but _not_ to speed up the ALU, so it's wrong to say the 68040 is "double-clocked." In a two-part 1990 article in _IEEE Micro_, Motorola explains that "Pclk provides timing reference points within each Bclk period," employing it for synchronous sub-cycle timing, and furthermore explicitly states that "all internal operations cycle at the Bclk rate." Still, the fact this clock signal was present at all gave Apple an excuse to tout _both_ timings for '040 Macintoshes, and Alpha Micro cheerfully reported just the faster one, even though the chip only _appears_ to run at that comparative speed from its larger 4K L1 cache, unhindered ALU and reduced cycles per instruction.
On this board, `Pclk` is provided by the same 80MHz crystal we saw on the AM-172, divided down by two to yield `Bclk` in the same way the 68EC030 board does for its single 40MHz clock. (For the E400's AM-174-00, this crystal would have been 66MHz divided down to 33MHz.) The single parity FPM SIMM slot and 16MHz and 50MHz oscillators are also present, as well as the same 53C710 SCSI controller, here a genuine NCR part. However, new for this board is 32K of L2 cache at the upper right/northeast corner, implemented with two IDT 71B74 8K cache-tag RAMs together providing 29 bits (512MB) of address comparison, and then four Cypress CY78C185 8K SRAMs for the cache itself. Remember, however, that in AMOS all cache is I-cache.
Effectively this 40/80MHz AM-174 makes our new system a full Eagle _500_, so why is it labeled as "only" an E300? I don't how how these systems originally shipped from the factory nor whether the E500 designation actually appeared on the back, but Alpha Micro did run a promotion in late 1997 where you could upgrade any Roadrunner '030 to a Roadrunner '040 by swapping the CPU board. My guess is this is one of those systems, and because that upgrade kit wouldn't have changed the plate on the back itself, the reseller simply noted it to be a working E300 and sold it to me as such. _It tried to boot._
Startled, I powered it off, connected the everything console, and turned it back on with the reset button held in to force a self-test. Except for the missing hard disk, _it passed the self-test_ — even the SCSI controller tested good.

This was clearly new behaviour — beforehand, it wouldn't do anything, not even enter the self-test, let alone attempt booting. Recall that error 2d had _two_ mentions in the manual, the second one referencing the primary and secondary boot devices. Since the self-test said the SCSI controller was fine, this made me suspicious that there was something about the ZuluSCSI's configuration the machine didn't like. [![](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgc17fcKHkQxq5KffcJTNhqZD2iebI9SsKBHRX5Rfl4BoPVIj5YXC5aAPfPLwjwy5Q7WR9kARfGRdl6Yea-ujT08Dggu8SP6yyZ_8Tq7sRWqX3IMqnLTEg76ntYeRqGmD1Xv2I9-b5DP3-UJJfB1PeGd0fjCc0G16YvYiDNrI07SqLCXU6fLJGVLlDvPnE/s320/PXL_20260906_213413592.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgc17fcKHkQxq5KffcJTNhqZD2iebI9SsKBHRX5Rfl4BoPVIj5YXC5aAPfPLwjwy5Q7WR9kARfGRdl6Yea-ujT08Dggu8SP6yyZ_8Tq7sRWqX3IMqnLTEg76ntYeRqGmD1Xv2I9-b5DP3-UJJfB1PeGd0fjCc0G16YvYiDNrI07SqLCXU6fLJGVLlDvPnE/s4080/PXL_20260906_213413592.jpg)
Now with my three main systems converted to solid state, I decided to stack them and save a bit of space, using the AM-1200 as a crossbar to support the AM-65 and AM-75 terminal heads and the E300 and E450 as its "legs." The E450 and AM-1200 share the AM-65; the E300, as the always-on server, gets the AM-75 all to itself. I suppose I'll find out sooner or later how seismically stable this is.
[![](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEi80fh7Ml7Ej6qh32X5mVxmhv858GhM-EmVFXNpXGaNs5LAVtG3q4oxTf3oUTFTm36Mvxfdp0PX4bpiNgDGlbUx1c1GKHFwzo939N4SYN-nvVRfp_08Me6AMp_-cWoZXEoh23SsZKrDz3d3vpNEKZm1RLWjhYd7uW6xKnRGPqqPP65-7yw3O2IK_yjkO24/s320/PXL_20260905_214604101.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEi80fh7Ml7Ej6qh32X5mVxmhv858GhM-EmVFXNpXGaNs5LAVtG3q4oxTf3oUTFTm36Mvxfdp0PX4bpiNgDGlbUx1c1GKHFwzo939N4SYN-nvVRfp_08Me6AMp_-cWoZXEoh23SsZKrDz3d3vpNEKZm1RLWjhYd7uW6xKnRGPqqPP65-7yw3O2IK_yjkO24/s4080/PXL_20260905_214604101.jpg)
That left our new arrival, the E500. I converted it to a ZuluSCSI Blaster as well because I was interested to see if the second-run speed bump would occur there also, given it has the same SCSI controller and the same general architecture as the E300. Annoyingly, when I extracted the Seagate Barracuda ST32272N hard disk from the 5.25" bay, one of the posts of the 3.5"-to-5.25" converter was broken and the LED cable hadn't been connected, though it won't fit the Blaster's LED header anyway.
[![](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEh-s4dqntYfouRD7br5TAtDA1GxwjXkyNw6xMk5AssZqQK7Mib1cf7gkCAv31kZo1Ue3F8pIB4ZQB3B7NmYA4eBFTdHvCGCwmLFvEQXPdvBi5JaGZHMcgvpK8DOwZapj6SYgwumNSP8PZWjVQ7MtATkWX1rT0fTjBF6XRuS646OYErz6dNueiHTx-FiyOQ/s320/PXL_20260906_003147026.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEh-s4dqntYfouRD7br5TAtDA1GxwjXkyNw6xMk5AssZqQK7Mib1cf7gkCAv31kZo1Ue3F8pIB4ZQB3B7NmYA4eBFTdHvCGCwmLFvEQXPdvBi5JaGZHMcgvpK8DOwZapj6SYgwumNSP8PZWjVQ7MtATkWX1rT0fTjBF6XRuS646OYErz6dNueiHTx-FiyOQ/s4080/PXL_20260906_003147026.jpg)
The first order of business was thus to solder some female Dupont jumpers onto the end of the activity LED wires so we could connect it.
[![](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjdx3CmuAAa077VJrIQ3W8XlCVF_IupnbkIwhp0euQOzQu0Bu8MIKthIPQQNlhXr5RRV3KNgCCssVD-wYAKxboVUamZjQQJ6hyk7VtF9SQmSIxufq34dyaaoou8Opz3IQNt2Ra4O8a-3KOqyfzgre0UfypyxjzKxYKjjvR-vkGasOKDzB2x-TZPNP7KFuw/s320/PXL_20260906_005155542~2.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjdx3CmuAAa077VJrIQ3W8XlCVF_IupnbkIwhp0euQOzQu0Bu8MIKthIPQQNlhXr5RRV3KNgCCssVD-wYAKxboVUamZjQQJ6hyk7VtF9SQmSIxufq34dyaaoou8Opz3IQNt2Ra4O8a-3KOqyfzgre0UfypyxjzKxYKjjvR-vkGasOKDzB2x-TZPNP7KFuw/s4080/PXL_20260906_005155542~2.jpg)
Now to mount it. I didn't have any more metal struts from the SGI Indigo^2, and I didn't have any screws that fit the plastic enclosure that would mate with the side rails, so I went with zipties. I said don't judge.
[![](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiNmqkL2cIOfNMkjK2fwnZovqJfnOVOY25ZOrvBwbNRjrkLQeI8cFuyFQ_uob_9kYyvG_7JCOEXCVAK-6GGo2NKU6JA2dkvJ8iXC9rYG573KxN81J2JGM2B4YsWUSE0oFoI4CjWloOmBivfbVXRoEACjr6epcERbgo_WPLbyFsGvDcMDIQl6hYRpsxTtPU/s320/PXL_20260906_011621952.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiNmqkL2cIOfNMkjK2fwnZovqJfnOVOY25ZOrvBwbNRjrkLQeI8cFuyFQ_uob_9kYyvG_7JCOEXCVAK-6GGo2NKU6JA2dkvJ8iXC9rYG573KxN81J2JGM2B4YsWUSE0oFoI4CjWloOmBivfbVXRoEACjr6epcERbgo_WPLbyFsGvDcMDIQl6hYRpsxTtPU/s4080/PXL_20260906_011621952.jpg)
Installed, as good as we can get, with the old LED connector for comparison.
[![](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiSl-LqzZraxduxn5vr0QaEPcPoQuqKpacr37pxgD_U3lKYuGr5MxzKf-TmSPHDcbxlvcrrK5p4M3rsrGv7q1Pjf98cBy48FyEDUb_rj9HFwZ1ts0liwZhYXO5VG2lUyIsU6vbMAZC-5-3jCkqCKTDGSZPNCDjOJPufiJT4zHwf7rn_iYpidNuS8zieOoE/s320/PXL_20260906_013313886.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiSl-LqzZraxduxn5vr0QaEPcPoQuqKpacr37pxgD_U3lKYuGr5MxzKf-TmSPHDcbxlvcrrK5p4M3rsrGv7q1Pjf98cBy48FyEDUb_rj9HFwZ1ts0liwZhYXO5VG2lUyIsU6vbMAZC-5-3jCkqCKTDGSZPNCDjOJPufiJT4zHwf7rn_iYpidNuS8zieOoE/s4080/PXL_20260906_013313886.jpg)
Since the zipties are only in the front, the board will swing down, but this is actually useful because I can easily access the configuration switches when the SCSI cable is unplugged. Like the E300, termination power is enough to run the ZuluSCSI in the E500, so there's no power cable to get in the way.
[![](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjKQiUYRrw_KjHDCF1zk_vxakmNJM5Uy_xEbJhou0g3UxlnOB3DGprrzFXiZ-uABfw0LSvR-ITpOtx8Ja2SxAfrPyMtyxBU8bA2J-csoUZWzvxueyJDisUgKE0Oxmv7zHE8xVHOgK_ahgmQOGYSdoIP-u8n2_uDDm1eJA8et_tezdglYuTZhIfYbjfGhG8/s320/PXL_20260906_013511579.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjKQiUYRrw_KjHDCF1zk_vxakmNJM5Uy_xEbJhou0g3UxlnOB3DGprrzFXiZ-uABfw0LSvR-ITpOtx8Ja2SxAfrPyMtyxBU8bA2J-csoUZWzvxueyJDisUgKE0Oxmv7zHE8xVHOgK_ahgmQOGYSdoIP-u8n2_uDDm1eJA8et_tezdglYuTZhIfYbjfGhG8/s4080/PXL_20260906_013511579.jpg)
When the SCSI cable is reattached, its connection to the tape streamer keeps it in raised position.
[![](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhCEtng-5PMWe6zNuZ3Y2ciM0ptDJgRGAVLq-cwyQMSxSLtYRnRVBVZbNPEEm_ZHKmidHw8TqMpKeS8FEIE7Eo0Bh3ba-0kM9UX876sIflaupezvkoAoXAT9u2YhjASlpXhJZBiy7fpH3texMfC_olQZ0YVs9wg7OVPrTBk46o5kg0jfFwv2HMJqhFWMZw/s320/PXL_20260906_195342340.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhCEtng-5PMWe6zNuZ3Y2ciM0ptDJgRGAVLq-cwyQMSxSLtYRnRVBVZbNPEEm_ZHKmidHw8TqMpKeS8FEIE7Eo0Bh3ba-0kM9UX876sIflaupezvkoAoXAT9u2YhjASlpXhJZBiy7fpH3texMfC_olQZ0YVs9wg7OVPrTBk46o5kg0jfFwv2HMJqhFWMZw/s4080/PXL_20260906_195342340.jpg)
The rear DIP switches were already correctly set, so the last step was to put its outer metal shell back on (a bit banged up though I managed to bend out a few of the defects) and give it a good scrub. I might consider Retr0brighting it later but simply cleaning it up made it look quite a bit better.
[![](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhDssUWLCCrvQPENqAEBelKJtm7rUB1_AFYcUCNg06WEXz9C38ywBH8BtMQ14MhcfG6wtnpMP-jcSc2ChH4y7GqKZlxD3-8LQk7GWbBtYNeYzwNIJ62vTnk6J37t2CoVFLz0kPAQET83StT6Kbc0lBn7Q3NQLVdqwoc0OdJLbk3jaity-frohps4e3q8pE/s320/PXL_20260906_211405754.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhDssUWLCCrvQPENqAEBelKJtm7rUB1_AFYcUCNg06WEXz9C38ywBH8BtMQ14MhcfG6wtnpMP-jcSc2ChH4y7GqKZlxD3-8LQk7GWbBtYNeYzwNIJ62vTnk6J37t2CoVFLz0kPAQET83StT6Kbc0lBn7Q3NQLVdqwoc0OdJLbk3jaity-frohps4e3q8pE/s4080/PXL_20260906_211405754.jpg)
Booting with the ["everything console."](/2026/06/building-serial-and-vga-everything.html) I should point out that the E500 has a slightly later version of AMOS than the E300 and E450 and we get a little more explanation with the bus readout:
``` .scsi Dispatched SCSI port:
SCSI id 7: (reserved) SCSI bus host adaptor SCSI id 6: SCSI-2 (tape) TANDBERG TDC 4100 0801=:CREATED12119 CmdQue Asynchronous SCSI id 5: No device or unable to report SCSI id 4: No device or unable to report SCSI id 3: No device or unable to report SCSI id 2: No device or unable to report SCSI id 1: No device or unable to report SCSI id 0: SCSI-2 (disk) ZULUSCSIHARDDRIVE 2.3BZuluSCSI CmdQue Synchronous: 10.00MB\8
```
While all three systems support synchronous SCSI, this version of AMOS actually reports it, along with the width (8-bit, because it's only Fast SCSI, not Wide). Now, what about performance?
``` .si dsk0: SI--AMOS System Information, (C) Copyright 1990, Alpha Microsystems Inc. Version 3.0(115)-1
Computer Type: Eagle Main Processor: 68040 Co-Processor: 68882 MMU present: Yes Operating System: AMOS 2.3A(489) Boot PROM revision: Unknown Number of SSDs: 1 Total Memory: 32768 K-bytes Resident Monitor Memory: 25249 K-bytes
Computing Index (CX), relative to AM-100: 83.8 48 bit FP Index (4X), relative to AM-100: 34.1 Floating Point Index (FX), relative to AM-100/L: 1700.0 Disk Index (DX), relative to ST-506: 46.3 .si dsk0: [...] Disk Index (DX), relative to ST-506: 180.7 .
```
The ST32272N we replaced is a 7200rpm drive while the ST310151N in the E300 was only 5400rpm, thus accounting for the E500's better baseline disk score, and the E500's faster CPU probably explains its slightly higher first-run result of 46.3. But the second run is even more lopsided than what we saw with the E300, a massive 180.7.
Since two of the systems were doing it, it was time to dig in a little more. The ZuluSCSI Blaster has a debug mode switch which echoes status and current operation to a connected machine over USB serial at 115200bps, so I hooked up both the E500's serial console and the USB port of the Blaster simultaneously to the MacBook Air to watch what SCSI operations occurred during the benchmark test.
[![](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhjXTAg-2wiju1JrcgoA4UZKb8Vuo8llcmkfRMB9spdxXcN7FjsaSk02ZNxsCilx8f1xvtH-Keg5nOGfvExw1d8mZtjXsxRcwRbiZ8Y8wqzQHwoN8b9pYgiKSC6NrKzL9pKUWrXf_50xMU_Q0Ol9Yv-g4qBUzUUbosdLb5dAKqasTf6nrzmkyYdpTyx7qY/s320/PXL_20261010_230411596.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhjXTAg-2wiju1JrcgoA4UZKb8Vuo8llcmkfRMB9spdxXcN7FjsaSk02ZNxsCilx8f1xvtH-Keg5nOGfvExw1d8mZtjXsxRcwRbiZ8Y8wqzQHwoN8b9pYgiKSC6NrKzL9pKUWrXf_50xMU_Q0Ol9Yv-g4qBUzUUbosdLb5dAKqasTf6nrzmkyYdpTyx7qY/s4080/PXL_20261010_230411596.jpg)
Debug mode obviously substantially impacts SCSI throughput because now the processor in the ZuluSCSI has to emit serial debugging information while it's satisfying requests, but SCSI activity during the first run didn't seem unusual. On the other hand, the activity during the second run was _very_ unusual: there wasn't any. In fact, even though the baseline score had sunk down to a dismal 10 or so because of all the debugging data it was emitting, the second run was still a blistering 180.7.
This really sounded like operating system caching, but except for the AM-1200 where I wasn't running it to save memory, the other three systems were running the standard disk cache as virtually any performance Alpha Micro would — and allegedly `SI.LIT` should be unswayed by it. For some reason the E450's cache configuration wasn't locking UFDs (user file directories, i.e., PPNs), but turning that off on the E500 and E300 didn't make a difference, and all three were caching everything else including the MFD (master file directory). However, when I turned off caching altogether at runtime (using the `CACHE.LIT` tool and disabling with `OFF`), though the scores got really low, they were now consistent from run to run.
Do note our observation isn't enough to fully explain the E450, which also runs the OS disk cache, but didn't have a second run bump. If you disable the cache on the E450, although its overall score declines, it still remains consistent from run to run. One possibility is that the driver for its later SCSI controller just isn't as aggressive.
Although the overall issue certainly calls into question how useful `SI.LIT` is as a disk benchmark, despite being likely the only Alpha Micro benchmark tool you can expect most recent systems to come with, the question then becomes _how_ comparative disk performance on an Alpha Micro should be measured. Was it still fine for me to continue with my usual practice of leaving the cache on and testing immediately after boot? It's probable that there'd be little in the cache by that point, whatever would be there would likely be similar from system to system (assuming the same version of the operating system), and likelier still that whatever _was_ present in the cache wouldn't be very germane to `SI.LIT`. Under my current knowledge of AMOS I think these numbers are still broadly comparable; I just have to keep in mind that the score on subsequent runs is likely to be bogus.
[![](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhSjU0D4ZX7RVt97K3IS9T9QRPPcXtPQe3IrUPf1SRl5e95CvyM5KP9gDRSGqhGk2hocVVNkZG0bvJ13BFjNu7Ds4YOfC9ogInH5blPo1zd-vrunOKp8C3L6bMHGhWdjJQsErY9hR1QhfVldyfKRWq4czq0swiR8CTjTLWsKSg-rjKq0-jTFALi8OqtLPg/s320/PXL_20260906_212817330.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhSjU0D4ZX7RVt97K3IS9T9QRPPcXtPQe3IrUPf1SRl5e95CvyM5KP9gDRSGqhGk2hocVVNkZG0bvJ13BFjNu7Ds4YOfC9ogInH5blPo1zd-vrunOKp8C3L6bMHGhWdjJQsErY9hR1QhfVldyfKRWq4czq0swiR8CTjTLWsKSg-rjKq0-jTFALi8OqtLPg/s4080/PXL_20260906_212817330.jpg)
With our Alpha Micro stack now in operation, shown here from the E300's console as it continues serving the world as it did before, let's briefly finish the story of the Eagles. The E100 and E450 became the basis for a number of even smaller systems used as network servers (e.g., the E100NX with few, if any, directly attached terminals) fed by network-connected terminal servers (e.g., E100TX, E450TX) based on the same platform. The single board systems were much cheaper to manufacture, and Alpha Micro discontinued the E300, E500 and E550 in 2000 to introduce the MCF5102-based E250, a cost-reduced E450 in the same way the E100 was a cost-reduced E300, running exactly the same processor at the same speed (Alpha Micro themselves reported a CX score of 59.9, precisely even with our E450 here). The E100 was discontinued shortly afterwards in 2001.
For Alpha Micro, the end of their 68K architecture systems was ultimately tied to the end of the 68K architecture generally. Motorola had never planned to evolve the MCF5102 further as it was always meant as a stopgap, and later ColdFires were not sufficiently suitable nor compatible to run the software legacy AMOS users ran. Although Alpha Micro's Falcon line of PC compatibility cards used them as a CPU starting with the 2002 PCI SuperFalcon (AM-113), it soon became clear PCs were fast enough for software emulation to be a far more effective option. In 2003 Alpha Micro introduced the AM-8000, an AMD Athlon PC running Windows XP Embedded with an on-board SuperFalcon, but here the SuperFalcon was demoted to a coprocessor for handling the SSD and terminal I/O running a reduced "Embedded AMOS" monitor. Everything else was an efficient software emulation, yielding a `SI.LIT` CX score of 816 (!) on dual Athlon 2800+ CPUs. Later AM-113 SuperFalcons were just serial ports and a socket for the SSD; the main system was now more than suitable to service them, and Motorola wasn't making any more 5102 CPUs either. The Eagle 800 that same year ran the same technology in miniature, bringing the great experiment to a close with the discontinuation of the last E250 and E450 systems, and today's systems sold by the reformulated Alpha Microsystems LLC use the same x86-based architecture.
Over their production lifetime, analysis of known serial numbers suggests around ten thousand 68K Eagles were ultimately sold, and now I've got five of them. Rest in peace, Rod. They're still great machines.
